descriptionChirho: The primary active sense of the verb חָפַשׂ in Qal and Piel stems, denoting a thorough, diligent search or investigation. Used of searching for persons (Gen 31:35; Gen 44:12), searching for enemies (1 Sam 23:23), searching out iniquities (Ps 64:7), examining one's ways (Lam 3:40), and God's searching of Jerusalem with lamps (Zeph 1:12). Multilingual evidence is highly consistent: Arabic فَتَّشَ/بَحَثَ (searched/investigated), German durchsuchte, Korean 뒤졌다/찾다 (rummaged/searched), Spanish buscó/escudriña, Hindi खोजा/ढूँढ़ा (searched/sought). The Piel intensifies the thoroughness of the search.

The Nifal and Pual passive forms of חָפַשׂ indicating being subjected to a thorough search or investigation by others. Includes the Pual participle מְחֻפָּשׂ meaning 'well-searched-out' (Ps 64:7), the Pual imperfect יְחֻפַּשׂ 'is searched for' (Prov 28:12), and the Nifal perfect נֶחְפְּשׂוּ 'have been searched' (Obad 1:6). Multilingual glosses confirm passive semantics: Arabic فُتِّش (was searched), German wurde durchsucht, Korean 수색되었느냐 (was it searched?), Spanish fue escudriñado, Japanese 探し出された (was searched out), Chinese 被搜查了 (was investigated).

The Hitpael reflexive sense of חָפַשׂ meaning to change one's own appearance so as not to be recognized, used exclusively of kings going into battle incognito or otherwise concealing their identity. Occurrences include Ahab disguising himself at Ramoth-Gilead (1 Kgs 20:38; 22:30; 2 Chr 18:29) and Josiah before his fatal battle (2 Chr 35:22). Multilingual evidence is highly uniform: Arabic تَنَكَّرَ (disguised), Korean 변장하였다/변장했다 (disguised), Spanish se disfrazó (disguised himself), Hindi भेस बदल/भेष बदला (changed disguise). Distinct from the disfigurement sense by its volitional, deliberate character.

labelChirho: to be disfigured, changed beyond recognition
descriptionChirho: A specialized Hitpael usage of חָפַשׂ in Job 30:18, describing involuntary disfigurement or alteration of appearance through disease or suffering, distinct from the deliberate self-disguise sense. The context is Job lamenting how his garment is disfigured and clings to him due to his affliction. English 'is disfigured,' Arabic يَتَنَكَّرُ (is altered), Korean 변한다 (is changed), Spanish se disfraza (is disguised), Hindi बदल गया है (has changed). Though morphologically identical to the disguise Hitpael, the involuntary, pathological nature of this transformation warrants a separate lexical sense.
